The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has criticised the Federal Government’s announcement of a N50,000 monthly cash relief payment, describing it as an election gimmick allegedly driven by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s desperation ahead of the 2027 general election.
The opposition party accused the Tinubu administration of attempting to regain public goodwill through cash handouts after subjecting Nigerians to severe economic hardship through its policies.
In a statement signed by its National Publicity Secretary, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the ADC questioned the timing of the announcement, alleging that the intervention was a reaction to the party’s promise to reduce the cost of living and make life more affordable if elected into power in 2027.
According to the party, the government has recently announced several intervention programmes without delivering meaningful relief to Nigerians.
“President Tinubu is in full panic mode now. Since the ADC and our Presidential Candidate, Atiku Abubakar, have made affordability and reducing the cost of living the cardinal focus of our campaign, the government has been announcing one desperate intervention or another,” Abdullahi said.
The party recalled the August announcement of a $1 billion Renewed Hope Social Intervention Fund, a proposed 30-day fuel discount, cheaper transportation across states from October 1, and a N70,000 transportation allowance for workers.
It alleged that these announcements had failed to translate into meaningful improvements in the living conditions of Nigerians.
The ADC also questioned the purchasing power of the proposed N50,000 payment, asking what meaningful assistance the amount could provide to households struggling with rising food, transportation, fuel and healthcare costs.
“What exactly is N50,000 supposed to buy in Tinubu’s Nigeria today? How much food can a family purchase with that amount? How much transport can it cover? And for how long?” the statement queried.
The party argued that petrol prices had increased significantly, with food and transportation costs also rising, making the proposed intervention inadequate to address the financial difficulties facing ordinary Nigerians.
It further accused the Federal Government of failing to anticipate the hardship associated with its economic reforms, insisting that vulnerable citizens should not have to wait until an election season to receive financial assistance.
According to the ADC, the government should have incorporated adequate social protection measures into its economic reform plans from the beginning rather than introducing cash relief programmes after years of economic difficulties.
The party also raised concerns about transparency and accountability in the implementation of government intervention programmes, warning that the latest initiative could create another avenue for the diversion of public funds.
It referenced findings attributed to the Auditor-General concerning previous cash transfer programmes, questioning whether billions of naira allocated to earlier interventions had been properly accounted for.
“What has happened to the findings of the Auditor-General concerning the billions of naira in previous cash transfers that could not be properly accounted for? Have those responsible been held accountable?” the party asked.
The ADC further questioned how Nigerians could be expected to trust another intervention programme when concerns surrounding previous government-funded initiatives had allegedly not been adequately addressed.
It warned that the N50,000 payment could either be an election-season publicity exercise intended to influence public perception or another programme vulnerable to financial mismanagement.
“At best, this is an election gimmick designed to deceive Nigerians into believing that a government which has neglected them for more than three years suddenly cares about their welfare. At worst, it could become another scheme to siphon public funds under the convenient cover of poverty alleviation,” the statement added.
The opposition party maintained that sustainable solutions to Nigeria’s cost-of-living crisis must go beyond temporary cash transfers.
It called for policies aimed at restoring citizens’ purchasing power and reducing the cost of essential commodities, particularly food, energy and transportation.
The ADC insisted that meaningful economic relief would require addressing the underlying causes of rising living costs rather than relying on periodic financial interventions.
The statement was signed by Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, National Publicity Secretary of the African Democratic Congress.
